source: Thaler & Sunstein (2008) Nudge, definition (read via Wikipedia Nudge theory page)
finding: A nudge is any part of the choice architecture that changes behaviour in a predictable way without banning options or changing incentives. It must be cheap and easy to avoid. Fruit at eye level is a nudge; a junk-food ban is not.
numbers: No numbers in the definition. Secondary summary [V via Wikipedia].
quote: any aspect of the choice architecture that alters people's behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options
limits: The definition is broad: any layout choice is a nudge. Choice architecture cannot be avoided, because something must be shown first.
agent_relevance: Every prompt is a choice architecture for the model. There is no neutral layout, only a chosen one. The schema should pick layouts on purpose and then check them.

source: Johnson & Goldstein (2003) Do defaults save lives? Science 302:1338
finding: Countries with opt-out organ donation have far higher consent than opt-in countries. A web experiment gave the same pattern.
numbers: From memory, not re-read this session: effective consent opt-in Denmark 4.25%, UK 17.17%, Germany 12.0%, Netherlands 27.5%; opt-out Austria 99.98%, Hungary 99.97%, France 99.91%, Belgium 98%, Poland 99.5%. Lab: opt-out about 82%, neutral about 79%, opt-in about 42%.
limits: Cross-country data is correlational. Later work found registered consent is not the same as actual donation, so the real gain is smaller. Verify figures before citing.
agent_relevance: Defaults are the strongest layout lever in humans. The model analogue is the pre-filled or first-offered answer in a prompt.

source: Madrian & Shea (2001) The power of suggestion: inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior (NBER 7682)
finding: A large US firm switched new hires from opt-in to automatic enrolment. Nothing economic changed. Participation jumped.
numbers: About 86% of the automatic-enrolment (NEW) cohort participated vs about half of the earlier WINDOW cohort. At equal tenure (3-15 months) the gap in non-participation was 48.5 percentage points.
limits: One firm, one time window, cohort comparison, not randomised. Tenure matched only on the 3-15 month window.
agent_relevance: A default carries the in/out choice and the details of the choice. Any default value we put into a prompt may be copied.

source: Madrian & Shea (2001) default contribution rate and fund
finding: The default was sticky on the details too. The firm default was 3% in a money market fund. Many people kept both, although almost nobody chose that mix before.
numbers: 76% of NEW-cohort participants contributed exactly 3% (about 10% in other cohorts). 80% of contributions went to the money market fund (16% to stock funds) vs about 70% to stock funds in other cohorts. 61% of the NEW cohort sat at 3% plus 100% money market, vs 1% in older cohorts.
limits: The default may also be read as advice. The paper cannot separate inertia from endorsement.
agent_relevance: A default value can anchor a whole answer, not just yes/no. Do not put a sample answer or value in a prompt unless we want it copied.

source: Thaler & Benartzi (2004) Save More Tomorrow, J Political Economy 112:S164
finding: Pre-commit people to raise saving at each future pay rise. Mechanism: loss aversion, inertia and limited self-control.
numbers: From memory, not re-read: 78% of those offered joined; saving rate rose from 3.5% to 13.6% over 40 months in the first firm.
limits: Few firms, mostly one case. Later results show smaller gains. Treat as an upper bound; verify.
agent_relevance: Pre-commitment design: fix the plan before the heat of the moment. Like locking checks and order in code before the model sees the problem.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) The framing of decisions, Science 211:453 (Asian disease numbers via Wikipedia Framing effect page)
finding: Asian disease problem: 600 people at risk. The same programs described as lives saved or lives lost flip preferences.
numbers: Gain frame: 72% chose the sure program (200 saved). Loss frame: 78% chose the risky program (1/3 chance nobody dies). Secondary summary; original paper not re-read.
limits: Replications confirm the direction but size varies with wording and sample. Meta-analyses (Kuhberger 1998, from memory) found a smaller average effect.
agent_relevance: Same facts, different frame, different answer. The cleanest human test to run on a model with S1 masking: restate the problem neutrally and see if answers move.

source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979) prospect theory; Tversky & Kahneman (1992) cumulative prospect theory
finding: Formal model behind framing: value is judged as gain or loss from a reference point; losses weigh more; probabilities are weighted.
numbers: From memory: loss aversion lambda about 2.25; curvature alpha about 0.88; probability weight gamma about 0.61 for gains.
limits: Parameters vary by sample. The theory does not say what sets the reference point; the frame does.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule: framing works by moving the reference point. A masking step that states a neutral reference should remove it.

source: Thaler & Shefrin (1981) planner-doer model; Kahneman (2011) System 1 and 2
finding: Nudges are explained by two selves: a fast automatic one that follows the default and a slow reflective one. Nudges aim at the fast one.
numbers: No numbers (conceptual model).
limits: Dual-process framing is contested; see the dual-process subfield in this series.
agent_relevance: Our schema already splits program and model. The layout can be fixed in code so the model's fast habits do not choose it.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: a meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions, PNAS 119:e2107346118
finding: The big meta-analysis of choice architecture finds a medium average effect.
numbers: 455 effect sizes, 214 publications, N = 2,149,683. Pooled Cohen d = 0.45 (95% CI 0.39-0.52). Egger test b = 2.28 (CI 1.31-3.25): publication bias.
limits: Authors called the bias moderate and did not correct the main estimate. Their sensitivity analysis allowed d as low as 0.08.
agent_relevance: Use d about 0.45 as the naive human prior and about 0.1 as the corrected one. Either way, test on the model directly.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) by technique and domain
finding: Decision-structure nudges (defaults, effort, option composition) beat information and assistance nudges. Food is the strongest domain, finance the weakest.
numbers: Structure d = 0.55 (k=227, N=357,179); assistance d = 0.31 (k=98); default d = 0.62 (k=132, CI 0.50-0.73); composition 0.55; effort 0.43; social reference 0.40. Food d = 0.72 (CI 0.49-0.95, N=12,515); finance 0.25 (CI 0.12-0.37); health 0.34.
limits: Moderators are correlated with each other and with publication bias.
agent_relevance: Structure beats information. For the agent: order and form of options matter more than extra advice text added to the prompt.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias, PNAS 119:e2200300119
finding: Re-analysis of the same data with robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA) removes almost all of the average effect.
numbers: Combined: random effects d = 0.43; RoBMA-PSMA d = 0.04 [0.00, 0.14]; using most precise estimates d = 0.11 [0.00, 0.24]. Information BF01 = 33.84 (for no effect); assistance BF01 = 9.05; structure adjusted d = 0.12 [0.00, 0.43], BF01 = 1.12 (undecided). Finance adjusted d = 0.00, BF01 = 41.23.
quote: when this publication bias is appropriately corrected for, no evidence for the effectiveness of nudges remains
limits: Evidence for heterogeneity in all categories except finance, so some nudges may work while the mean is near zero. Structure/default evidence is undecided, not refuted. Mertens and others replied that the correction is too severe.
agent_relevance: Report both numbers. The human effect for structure nudges is somewhere between d 0.1 and 0.6. Do not rest the design on the human effect size.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) RCTs to scale: comprehensive evidence from two nudge units, Econometrica 90:81 (NBER 27594)
finding: All trials from two US nudge units (not filtered by publication) show much smaller effects than the journal literature.
numbers: 126 RCTs, over 23 million people. Nudge units: 1.4 percentage points, an 8.1% increase. Published academic sample: 8.7 pp, a 33.5% increase.
limits: Authors say publication bias plus low power can explain the whole gap; nudge features (letters vs in-person) explain part. Only 2 trials were default changes, so defaults are barely tested at scale here.
agent_relevance: Real-world effect is about one fifth of the published one. Expect small noisy layout effects in agents too and measure with enough items.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) forecasts
finding: Experts expect nudges to work better than they do. Practitioners were closer than academics.
numbers: Median forecast for nudge-unit effect 4 pp (mean 5.8 pp); practitioners' median 1.95 pp; actual 1.4 pp.
limits: Small forecaster samples.
agent_relevance: Our own priors about layout effects on the model are probably too large. Write down the expected size first, then measure.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects, Behavioural Public Policy
finding: Default effects are reliable but depend on why the default works: implied endorsement, effort, or reference point.
numbers: From memory, not re-read: about 58 studies, N about 73,000, Cohen d about 0.68. Larger when the default signals endorsement.
limits: Not verified this session; cited in DellaVigna & Linos at their text on default changes. Publication bias was probed less than in Maier et al.
agent_relevance: Three mechanisms (endorsement, effort, reference point) map to LLM causes: instruction following, copy bias, prior over first tokens. Test which one.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Tested prompts for framing, group attribution, primacy, anchoring and status quo bias in admissions-officer tasks with GPT-4 and Llama-2 7B/13B.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing than under the admit framing. Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Primacy: options A and B were chosen more than C and D although equal. No human-like status-quo bias; for most models the status-quo option A was chosen less.
limits: Synthetic student profiles. Few-shot debiasing sometimes drove the admit rate to 0 or 1 (instruction failure).
agent_relevance: Framing and order both move LLM decisions. Defaults do not behave as in humans (reverse effect), so do not copy human nudge lore.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) debiasing results
finding: Self-help debiasing (the model rewrites the prompt to remove biased parts) worked best. Awareness prompts helped a little. Few-shot examples caused failures.
numbers: Remaining biased prompt elements after selfhelp: framing 0% (Llama 2 13B), 1.4% (Llama 2 7B), 2.7% (GPT-4); group attribution 0% (GPT-4); status quo 6% (Llama 2 7B), 0% (13B). Awareness reduced remaining framing/status quo to 17.2% and 8.5% in one model.
limits: Measures how many biased prompt parts were removed, not accuracy against ground truth.
agent_relevance: Supports S1 masking: restate the problem without loaded wording before solving. Needs a test that meaning is kept.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3, PNAS 120:e2218523120 (arXiv 2206.14576)
finding: GPT-3 on classic decision tasks shows the framing effect, the certainty effect and overweighting of small probability differences.
numbers: Three of the six Kahneman-Tversky prospect-theory effects replicated in GPT-3 (framing, certainty, small-probability weighting).
limits: GPT-3 only; vignettes may be in training data (authors warn). Small vignette changes threw it off.
agent_relevance: Frame sensitivity is a model trait, not only a human one. Re-check on current models; do not assume it persists.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? (GPT-3.5)
finding: ChatGPT showed anchoring, representativeness, availability, framing and endowment effects, like humans.
numbers: Framing study: ChatGPT rated a medicine 5 (1-7 scale) in all 11 positive-frame trials and 4 in all 11 negative-frame trials. Humans: 5.2 (CI 5.03-5.37) vs 4.6 (CI 4.35-4.85), t(80) = 3.86, p < 0.001.
limits: Only 11 trials with fixed output, so the model effect has no spread. GPT-3.5 only.
agent_relevance: The effect shows with no sampling noise: a layout effect is a bias, not a wobble, so majority voting will not remove it (G4).

source: Lu, Bartolo, Moore, Riedel, Stenetorp (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts and where to find them, ACL
finding: The order of few-shot examples swings accuracy between near state of the art and random guess. A good order for one model does not carry to another.
numbers: All 24 orderings of 4 examples on SST-2 and Subj, GPT-2 (0.1B-1.5B) and GPT-3 (up to 175B). Entropy-based probing-set selection gave about 13% relative improvement over eleven tasks. Cross-model correlation of order performance is near zero or negative in several pairs (e.g. -0.24).
limits: Older models and classification tasks. Newer instruction-tuned models are less sensitive but not immune.
agent_relevance: Never trust one example order. Use code to shuffle and compare, or pick order by a held-out check.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts, TACL (arXiv 2307.03172)
finding: The position of the relevant document gives a U-shaped accuracy curve: best at the start and end, worst in the middle.
numbers: Multi-document QA with 20 documents: GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy falls by more than 20% from best to worst position and in the middle goes below its closed-book accuracy of 56.1% (oracle 88.3%). Closed-book/oracle: Claude-1.3 48.3/76.1; MPT-30B 31.5/81.9; LongChat-13B 35.0/83.4. Longer-context versions did not fix it.
limits: 2023 models. Later long-context models are better, but position effects are reported still.
agent_relevance: Put key facts and rules at the start or end of the prompt and keep the evidence block short. Do not bury rules in the middle.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors, ICLR (PriDe)
finding: Models prefer certain option letters. The cause is mainly token bias on option IDs, not option content. Moving the golden answer to a slot shifts accuracy a lot.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. 0-shot MMLU: llama-30B 53.1 original; golden moved to A 68.2 (+15.2), to D 41.2 (-11.9). gpt-3.5-turbo 67.2 original; to D 60.9 (-6.3). Removing option IDs reduces selection bias.
limits: Mostly open models plus gpt-3.5. PriDe debiasing needs output probabilities.
agent_relevance: Use content labels, or cyclic permutation averaged in code (G5). A weaker model can beat a stronger one by answer position alone.

source: Pezeshkpour & Hruschka (2023) LLMs sensitivity to the order of options in multiple-choice questions
finding: Reordering options changes answers, also with few-shot demonstrations. Worst when the model is torn between its top two choices.
numbers: Sensitivity gap of about 13% to 75% across benchmarks when options are reordered; zero-shot gap up to 75%; with few-shot and accuracy above 90% a gap of 13.1% remained.
limits: 75% is a maximum on one benchmark/model, not typical.
agent_relevance: Order bias is largest when the model is unsure, so an answer that flips on reordering is a usable uncertainty signal (G1 trigger).

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design (FormatSpread), ICLR
finding: Meaning-preserving format changes (separators, casing, spacing) change accuracy a lot, and not in a way tied to model size or shots.
numbers: Accuracy range up to 76 points for LLaMA-2-13B between equivalent formats; about 10 points on average across 50+ tasks and several models. Persisted with more shots, larger model, or instruction tuning.
limits: Mostly open-weights models, classification-style tasks.
agent_relevance: Report results across a set of formats, never one. A single pilot layout can mislead by 10 points or more.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large language models are not fair evaluators (arXiv 2305.17926)
finding: When an LLM judges two responses, swapping their order flips the verdict.
numbers: Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries with ChatGPT as judge when the order favoured Vicuna. Fixes proposed: multiple evidence calibration, balanced position calibration, human-in-the-loop calibration.
limits: 80-query benchmark; early 2023 judges.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: no model judge without both orders and no authorship cues; average over both orders in code.

source: Nudge critiques: durability, ethics, heterogeneity (via Wikipedia Nudge theory page)
finding: Critics say effects are weaker in practice, averages hide large spread, and covert nudges may not last. Defence: choice architecture is unavoidable.
numbers: Cites Mertens (d about 0.45, moderate publication bias), Maier (no effect after correction) and a nudge-unit analysis over 23 million people with substantially weaker effects. Personalised nudges beat one-for-all.
limits: Secondary source; read the first 100,000 of 115,571 characters.
agent_relevance: The heterogeneity argument fits LLMs: some layouts matter a lot for some models and tasks, not for others. Measure per task and per model.
